History

The idea behind The Puck School grows out of the public subject it builds on. Its novelty is a swap rule: any robot can be swapped for another without changing the experiment, so results repeat. As a Signature design it is new work, drawn from the public record but not itself a public record: The School is meant for classrooms and labs that need honest comparisons. Its history is therefore the history of its design choices, recorded here so a reader can see why each part is the way it is.

Description

The Puck School is a Signature design-study: A Signature design for a school of identical puck robots that test swarm rules. The Puck School is a Signature-made design: a school of identical puck-shaped robots for testing swarm rules fairly. Its novelty is a swap rule: any robot can be swapped for another without changing the experiment, so results repeat. The School is meant for classrooms and labs that need honest comparisons. This is a Signature-made design, presented as a design study only, never as an established fact and never as a built product. The design is judged on its own terms: whether its rules are clear, its parts fit together, and its checks can be run.

The Problem

The problem The Puck School addresses is this: A Signature design for a school of identical puck robots that test swarm rules. The Puck School is a Signature-made design: a school of identical puck-shaped robots for testing swarm rules fairly. Without a design for it, the work is done ad hoc, with no shared language and no way to check the result. The design gives the work a shape that can be taught, tested and improved.

The Worked Solution

The worked solution has 5 steps, each of which can be checked on its own. Step 1: Place the pucks in the arena and load the rule. Step 2: Calibrate the sensors against the floor. Step 3: Run the rule and record every path from above. Step 4: Swap robots and repeat the run. Step 5: Report the behaviour and the repeatability. Running the steps in order produces the result reported below, and the checkable numbers are arena_m2 5, robots 14, runs 22, sensors 8, speed_cms 13, success_pct 94. Each step uses only the facts stated in this record, so a reader can follow the whole solution without outside knowledge.

The Answer

When The Puck School is followed, the result is a working design for A Signature design for a school of identical puck robots that test swarm rules. The checkable numbers for this record are arena_m2 5, robots 14, runs 22, sensors 8, speed_cms 13, success_pct 94, with a total of 156, a largest value of 94 and a smallest of 5. The demo recomputes those numbers twice and prints both digests, so the arithmetic can be checked by anyone.

When It Applies

The Puck School applies wherever A Signature design for a school of identical puck robots that test swarm rules. It applies as a design study: in teaching, in planning, and as a starting point for a build. It does not apply as a specification for buying, certifying or deploying anything, since it has not been built or tested.

Limits

The limits of The Puck School are the limits of a design study. It has not been built, tested in the field, or reviewed by outside experts, and its numbers are design numbers, not measurements. It must not be cited as evidence that any product exists or that any effect has been observed. What it can do is show a clear design, with parts that fit and checks that run, so a builder can judge whether it is worth building.

Math Proof

The mathematics of The Puck School is bookkeeping mathematics: the checkable figures are arena_m2 5, robots 14, runs 22, sensors 8, speed_cms 13, success_pct 94. Their total is 156, their largest is 94 and their smallest is 5. The demo adds them, averages them and hashes the result twice; if the two digests match, the arithmetic is deterministic, which is the whole mathematical claim this record makes.

Science Proof

The science behind The Puck School is design science: Its novelty is a swap rule: any robot can be swapped for another without changing the experiment, so results repeat. The School is meant for classrooms and labs that need honest comparisons. A design is good science when its claims are stated plainly, its limits are named, and its checks are runnable. This record states its claims as design claims only, and it names its limits in the Limits section, so no reader mistakes a design for a discovery.

Demo

The demo recomputes the checkable figures twice and prints both SHA-256 digests. Its captured output is stored in expected_output; run the demo to reproduce it.

Program

The program is a Python class with a run() method that recomputes the same result as the demo.

Generator

The seeded boundless generator for this database creates new records on demand from a seed number; the same seed always produces the same record. Generator ceiling: up to 1,000,000,000 scales per file, generated on demand by the file AI — not stored files.

AI

The AI for this database is JAH Swarm Robotics Librarian (Signature). It explains the database, answers questions from its own data, and routes harder questions to the master AI.

Terms in Plain Words

A database is a named collection of records about one subject, stored so a reader or a program can find, read, and check each record. A record is one entry in a database: a single file with all of its data, written so a person can read it and a program can run it. A slug is the short web-address name of a database, written in lower-case letters with hyphens, for example multi-robot-coordination. It is the name the database is filed under. The manifest is the master list of every database in the network, kept in data/manifest.json in the jah-databases repository. It records each database's slug, record kind, record count, identifier prefix, and AI name. A slug is free only if it is not already in the manifest. A record kind is the type name of a record, written as the database slug with spaces instead of hyphens, for example multi-robot coordination record. An identifier prefix is the short code stamped at the start of every record identifier in a database, for example JAH-MRCP-. It tells you which database a record belongs to. A generator is a program that creates new records or files on demand from a seed number. The same seed always produces the same output, so a generated record can be checked and reproduced. A seed is the starting number given to a generator. Change the seed and you get a different record; use the same seed and you get the same record again. A generator gate is a check that a generator must pass before its output counts: the emitted record must have the right record kind, the right slug, the database's own identifier prefix, the hard stop of 1,000,000,000, and the right generator prefix. A JCC code (JAH Condensed Code) is a short condensed key that points to one full record: JAHDB/<slug>#<id>, with a jcc_key of k= plus the first 8 characters of the SHA-256 digest of the record. A code is a pointer to the full data, never a replacement for it. An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules that lets one program ask another program for data or work, over the web. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets an AI program connect to outside tools and data sources through one shared set of rules. AI means artificial intelligence: a program that answers questions, explains things, and does work from data. SQLite is a small database stored as a single file on disk, read and written with the SQL language. SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for asking a database for records and for adding, changing, or removing them. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a plain-text way of writing structured data as named fields and lists, readable by people and programs. HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the language that marks up a web page: headings, paragraphs, lists, and links. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is the language that styles a web page: colours, layout, and type. A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is a web address: the full path that names one page, file, or resource on the web. HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the rule set a browser and a web server use to ask for and deliver web pages. HTTPS (HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) is HTTP with the connection encrypted, so the data cannot be read or changed in transit. A test suite is a set of checks run against a program to prove it does what it claims, including checks that a deliberate defect is caught. A demo is a small working program that runs the checkable part of a record twice and prints both SHA-256 digests, so anyone can see the result is deterministic. A lidar is a laser scanner that measures distances by timing light pulses. A photon is a single particle of light. Entanglement is a link between two quantum particles so that measuring one affects the other, even at a distance.

demo.code:
import hashlib
FIGURES = {'arena_m2': 5, 'robots': 14, 'runs': 22, 'sensors': 8, 'speed_cms': 13, 'success_pct': 94}
LABEL = 'swarm-robotics-laboratory-signature-000005'
def compute():
    vals = list(FIGURES.values())
    total = sum(vals)
    n = len(vals)
    mean = round(total / n, 4) if n else 0
    out = {"count": n, "label": LABEL, "max": max(vals), "mean": mean, "min": min(vals), "total": total}
    return out
outputs = compute()
result = "|".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in sorted(outputs.items()))
h1 = hashlib.sha256(result.encode()).hexdigest()
outputs2 = compute()
result2 = "|".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in sorted(outputs2.items()))
h2 = hashlib.sha256(result2.encode()).hexdigest()
for k, v in sorted(outputs.items()):
    print(f"{k}: {v}")
print(f"Result: {result}")
print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {h1}")
print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {h2}")
print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if h1 == h2 else 'MISMATCH'}")

import hashlib
class SwarmRoboticsLaboratorySignatureProgram:
    """Working program for this record; run() recomputes the demo result."""
    def run(self):
        import hashlib
        FIGURES = {'arena_m2': 5, 'robots': 14, 'runs': 22, 'sensors': 8, 'speed_cms': 13, 'success_pct': 94}
        LABEL = 'swarm-robotics-laboratory-signature-000005'
        def compute():
            vals = list(FIGURES.values())
            total = sum(vals)
            n = len(vals)
            mean = round(total / n, 4) if n else 0
            out = {"count": n, "label": LABEL, "max": max(vals), "mean": mean, "min": min(vals), "total": total}
            return out
        outputs = compute()
        result = "|".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in sorted(outputs.items()))
        h1 = hashlib.sha256(result.encode()).hexdigest()
        outputs2 = compute()
        result2 = "|".join(f"{k}={v}" for k, v in sorted(outputs2.items()))
        h2 = hashlib.sha256(result2.encode()).hexdigest()
        for k, v in sorted(outputs.items()):
            print(f"{k}: {v}")
        print(f"Result: {result}")
        print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {h1}")
        print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {h2}")
        print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if h1 == h2 else 'MISMATCH'}")
        return result
